candidates.title: The season's motto inverts a proverb — and matches an Auden title exactly
candidates.detail: Apple's season-four logline says Ted and the team learn to leap before they look, and Jason Sudeikis has framed the season around that inversion of 'look before you leap.' W.H. Auden published a poem titled 'Leap Before You Look' in 1940 (collected in The Double Man, 1941), whose subject is exactly this: that safety is an illusion and the leap has to be taken anyway. NO SOURCE FOUND connecting the show's phrase to Auden deliberately — the poem is real and the title match is exact, but intent is unestablished. Reviewer must decide whether to present it as resonance rather than reference.
candidates.moment: Not an on-screen moment — it is the season's stated framing, which this premiere sets up as Ted decides to uproot his life again without knowing how it lands.

sources.note: LEAD, NOT YET OPENED — Auden poem title, 1940 date, and theme of accepting risk

candidates.title: Leaping before you look is William James's precursive faith, restated
candidates.detail: The idea already anchoring this app's Season 1 cards — William James's precursive faith, belief that runs ahead of the evidence and helps bring about the thing believed in — is precisely what the season's 'leap before you look' framing names. Ted has no evidence the women's-team job will work; taking it is the bet, not the conclusion. Interpretive mapping by the hunter, built on the sourced James material in docs/factsheet.md (ch. 3, David Baggett), not on a claim any critic has made about this episode.
candidates.moment: Ted accepts a job rebuilding a second-division women's side from almost nothing, and moves his family across an ocean to do it, before there is any reason to think it will succeed.

sources.note: episode plot: Ted accepts the women's-team job and relocates

candidates.title: Higgins visits the Negro Leagues Baseball Museum
candidates.detail: While the Richmond contingent is in Kansas City, Higgins visits the Negro Leagues Baseball Museum — a real institution in KC's 18th & Vine district, commemorating the segregated leagues where players like Satchel Paige starred. Two recaps report the episode explicitly rhymes that history of a talent pool shut out of the resourced league with the modern underfunding of women's football, which is the argument the season is making.
candidates.moment: Higgins tours the museum and comes away with a sharpened sense of what a systematically under-resourced league does to the people playing in it.

candidates.title: The episode's argument: home is not one fixed place
candidates.detail: The title works on two meanings at once — Kansas, where Ted's family is, and Richmond, where he became himself. Multiple recaps converge on the same reading: the episode refuses the choice, and Ted's answer is to try to hold both by bringing his family with him rather than trading one for the other. Rebecca voices the thesis (paraphrase: sometimes home is a state of mind).
candidates.moment: Ted weighs Kansas against Richmond and lands on neither-as-a-sacrifice: he goes back, but not alone.

sources.note: home as continually redefined, not chosen once
Rebecca voices the 'state of mind' thesis
corroborates the both-not-either resolution

candidates.title: Dottie is selling the house Ted grew up in
candidates.detail: Per Wikipedia's episode page, Ted's interest in the Richmond offer sharpens after he learns his mother plans to sell his childhood home. It is the literal 'home' the title is punning on, and it removes the fixed point Ted was orbiting. Dottie Lasso (Becky Ann Baker) is a Season 3 returning character; the critical-myth reviewer flags that her stance here reads differently from her Season 3 position — reviewer should check whether that is a genuine inconsistency or growth, and NOT assert either.
candidates.moment: Ted learns the house he grew up in is going on the market, which reframes what staying in Kansas would even be preserving.

candidates.title: A man with nothing wrong in his life and nothing right either
candidates.detail: Ted is working at a Kansas City grocery store, present for Henry, and by every external measure fine — but reviewers describe him as existing rather than living, the coaching spark gone. That is the classic problem virtue ethics poses better than a happiness calculus does: Aristotle's question is not whether you are comfortable but whether you are exercising your characteristic capacity well. The show has always had a virtue-ethics spine (see ch. 6 of Ted Lasso and Philosophy). NOTE the sources disagree on Ted's exact job — Wikipedia says cashier, other recaps say assistant manager; card should say 'working at a grocery store' and no more.
candidates.moment: Ted is doing the thing he left England to do, and it is visibly not enough.

candidates.title: The show picked a new underdog on purpose
candidates.detail: The premise change is the argument: a second-division women's side, under-resourced by design, lets the series restate its original underdog setup with a real-world injustice underneath it. Recaps report the episode explicitly raises how women's programmes are defunded relative to men's — one names Twickenham FC's women's team as the in-episode example. Reviewer should verify whether Twickenham FC is a real club being invoked or an invented one, and NOT present it as real without checking.
